paragraphs.heading: Counting successes
paragraphs.text: Picture running the same yes-or-no experiment n times in a row. Each try is independent of the others, and each one comes out as a success with probability p or a failure with probability q = 1 − p. The binomial distribution tells you how likely each possible number of successes is across all n tries. If a random variable X behaves this way, we write X ~ B(n, p), where n is a natural number and p lies between 0 and 1.

paragraphs.heading: Built from Bernoulli trials
paragraphs.text: A single experiment that can only succeed or fail goes by the name Bernoulli trial, and a run of such outcomes is called a Bernoulli process. So the binomial distribution is really about a string of Bernoulli trials. With only one trial, when n = 1, it reduces to what is called the Bernoulli distribution. It also serves as the foundation of the binomial test, a tool for judging statistical significance.

paragraphs.heading: Where the formula comes from
paragraphs.text: Take one particular string of n trials holding k successes and n − k failures. The chance of seeing exactly that string is pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ. Since the trials are independent and the chances stay fixed from one trial to the next, every such string has this same probability, wherever the successes happen to sit. Printed tables of binomial probabilities usually only run up to n/2, because for k > n/2 you can get the value from its complement, since f(k; n, p) matches f(n − k; n, 1 − p).

paragraphs.heading: The typical outcome
paragraphs.text: For X ~ B(n, p), the expected value is E [X] = np, the number of trials times the chance of success on each. If np happens to be an integer, the mean, the median and the mode all land on that same value, np. With p = 0, getting zero successes is certain, and with p = 1, all n trials succeed, so the mode is 0 in the first case and n in the second.

paragraphs.heading: Estimating p from data
paragraphs.text: When the number of trials n is known, p can be estimated by the fraction of trials that succeeded, p̂ = x/n. Two standard routes give this same answer: maximum likelihood estimation and the method of moments. The estimate is unbiased and has minimum variance. For large samples it is approximately normal, thanks to the central limit theorem, since it amounts to averaging Bernoulli samples.

paragraphs.heading: With or without replacement
paragraphs.text: A common use is counting successes in a sample of size n taken with replacement from a population of size N. If the items are not put back, the draws stop being independent, and the count follows a hypergeometric distribution rather than a binomial one. Even so, when N is far bigger than n, the binomial still approximates the answer well, and it is widely used.
